newsitem.title: UK: Wide powers for UK transport/environment supremo.
newsitem.headline: Wide powers for UK transport/environment supremo.

text.p: Britain's Labour government put transport at the heart of its political agenda on Friday, with the new deputy prime minister John Prescott appointed as head of a new super-ministry embracing transport and the environment.
Prescott, son of a railway worker and a former steward on cruise ships, was appointed by new British prime minister Tony Blair as the minister in charge of the two portfolios on Friday.

Prescott's new remit will put a single minister in charge of the nationwide transport system, national building planning procedures and green issues such as pollution control -- a move which transport analysts cautiously welcomed.
Another big issue Labour faces is an unresolved transatlantic open-skies trade negotiation between Britain and the U.S.

An open skies agreement is a key condition for clearing the controversial proposed alliance between British Airways Plc and American Airlines. This deal also has to be vetted under Britain's competiton laws by Labour's new trade and industry minister, Margaret Beckett.
So far, Labour has said only that it will want to review the whole issue of open skies and the BA/American alliance.

On land transport, Prescott will take over a system which is now largely privatised, with the break-up of British Rail now completed and a thriving privatised bus sector in place after the deregulation which began 10 years ago.
The question for investors in the bus and rail operators is whether Prescott will be tempted to adopt a more interventionist approach.

Dr Stephen Glaister, transport analyst at the London School of Economics, told Reuters: "On the question of whether Labour wishes to unpick privatisation -- this is probably not feasible in the short term and there is not a lot to be gained. Instead, I do think we'll see tighter regulation."
Lynn Sloman, director of pressure group Transport 2000, also believed regulation would be key in dealing with privatised rail and bus industries.

Prescott and Andrew Smith, the party's shadow transport spokesman during opposition, have both talked of creating a single rail regulator with beefed up powers, instead of a currently fragmented system.
Sloman said she believed it could be modelled on Germany's Office of Rail Policy which combined strategic transport planning to encourage rail use as well as regulatory duties.
But she said Labour was unlikely to want to risk a more confrontational approach with the private sector.
"From what we've heard so far, it is clear that Labour wants to act in partnership with the private sector.
"It will sweet talk them rather than use the heavy-handed approach. But nonetheless it will signal that it expects cooperation on certain issues," she said.

The Association of Train Operating Companies, representing the 25 passenger rail private sector franchises, said in a statement: "The industry looks forward to a good working relationship with the new Labour government."
ATOC added it sought to "help the government develop its plans for the passenger railway for the overall benefit of the customer."

But Labour has fired a warning shot to business. In a pre-election interview with Reuters, Labour's ex-shadow transport spokesman Smith said it would clamp down on rail franchises which did not deliver service committments.
He also said Labour had set its sights on possibly using legislation to force Railtrack Plc, the privatised infrastructure company, to meet its investment obligations.

Glaister said the merger of the environment and transport ministries would allow government to coordinate planning for construction development with traffic management as well as bringing together overlapping areas of local government budgeting.
One key option being considered by Labour is giving local government powers to introduce road pricing or tolling and use the revenues to reinvest in reigonal transport.
Such a policy would be handled more efficiently under a joint ministry covering planning and transport needs.
"The phenomenal growth in traffic creates local problems requiring local solutions," said Glaister. Transport 2000 added "This will make a lot more sense."
Other challenges which will face Prescott include how to revitalise the crumbling London Underground metro or "tube" at a time when economic growth is set to put more pressure on the system.
Before the election Labour shunned the then ruling Conservatives' idea of privatisation of the tube.

The LSE's Glaister said Labour's current commitment to use private finance projects to meet the system's investment needs "would not solve the problem. The system needs a slug of extra subsidy otherwise we will see the overcrowding problems seen in the last boom."
One last issue is whether it will consider taking up its predecessor's commitment to privatise the Civil Aviation Authority.

In the election run-up Labour said it would not rule out privatisation as a matter of dogma, possibly leaving the door open at a time when the new government has submitted to the existing spending straitjacket.
